summary: The investigation did not identify a definitive root cause; the two leading hypotheses—resource exhaustion on ledger-db due to a traffic surge (confidence 0.60) and ledger-db connection pool saturation (confidence 0.50)—remain plausible. Verified observations show a sharp latency increase, statement timeouts, CPU >95%, and active connections rising to ~187, but key metrics (request rate, pool configuration) are missing. Immediate mitigations to reduce load and increase pool capacity are recommended, alongside data collection to discriminate between the hypotheses.

ranked_hypotheses.title: Resource exhaustion on ledger-db due to traffic surge
ranked_hypotheses.statement: A sudden increase in order-service request volume caused a surge of queries against ledger-db, driving active connections up and CPU to >95%, which resulted in statement timeouts and the observed order-service latency spike.

causal_chain.claim: Traffic surge on order-service increased DB query rate
Active DB connections rose from ~95 to ~187
CPU usage on ledger-db spiked to >95%
High CPU and connection count caused statement timeouts
Statement timeouts manifested as order-service p99 latency >5 s

assumptions: Order-service request rate increased sharply around 08:45‑09:00

ranked_hypotheses.title: Ledger-db connection pool saturation
ranked_hypotheses.statement: The ledger-db connection pool reached its maximum size, causing new queries to wait for a free slot; the resulting queuing led to statement timeouts and elevated order-service latency.

causal_chain.claim: Active connections grew to ~187, exceeding typical pool capacity
Queued queries timed out, producing 'statement timeout' errors
Order-service observed high latency and error rate

ranked_hypotheses.title: Autovacuum config change degraded ledger-db performance
ranked_hypotheses.statement: The reduction of autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor on ledger-db (cfg-2903) caused autovacuum to run less frequently, allowing table bloat and dead tuples to accumulate, which increased query execution cost, leading to CPU saturation and statement timeouts observed by order-service.

causal_chain.claim: Reduced autovacuum allowed table bloat / dead tuples to increase query cost
Higher query cost drove CPU usage >95% and active connections up, causing statement timeouts

assumptions: Table bloat increased sufficiently within <1 h after config change

ranked_hypotheses.title: Downstream pricing-engine slowdown cascaded to DB overload
ranked_hypotheses.statement: A slowdown in the pricing-engine service caused order-service request handling threads to block longer, increasing the duration of DB transactions and ultimately saturating ledger-db, leading to statement timeouts.

causal_chain.claim: Order-service threads waited longer for pricing responses, extending DB transaction time
Extended DB usage increased CPU and connection pressure on ledger-db
Resulted in statement timeouts and order-service latency

assumptions: Pricing-engine latency increased concurrently with DB metrics

facts.statement: Order-service latency (p99) jumped from ~150 ms to >800 ms at 08:52 and stayed >5 s through 10:52.
Order-service error logs contain "statement timeout" starting at 09:00:42.
Order-service error rate rose to ~9 % at 09:00.
Ledger-db CPU usage spiked to >95 % from 09:00 onward.
Ledger-db active connections rose from ~95 at 08:52 to ~187 at 09:00.
No WARN‑level autovacuum or lock‑contention logs were observed between 07:00 and 10:30.
Ledger-db disk usage remained steady (~71 %) and replication lag stayed ~40 ms during the incident.
A configuration change reduced autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor on ledger-db at 08:00 (cfg-2903).
Order-service directly accesses ledger-db (shared PostgreSQL datastore).

assumptions: Order-service request rate increased sharply around 08:45‑09:00 (required for H2).
Ledger-db connection pool maximum size is configured below 180 connections (required for H3).
Table bloat could have increased sufficiently within <1 h after the autovacuum config change (required for H1).
Pricing-engine latency did not change significantly during the incident (required for H4).

timeline.event: Autovacuum configuration change on ledger-db (vacuum_scale_factor reduced).
Order-service p99 latency jumps to >800 ms; ledger-db CPU spikes to 46.67 %; active connections rise to ~95.
Ledger-db CPU exceeds 95 %; active connections reach ~187; order-service error rate hits ~9 %; first statement timeout logs appear.
First "statement timeout" log entry recorded in order-service.
Order-service latency remains >5 s; ledger-db metrics stay at high CPU and connection levels.

recommended_actions.action: Temporarily throttle incoming order-service requests via api-gateway rate limiting to reduce DB load.
recommended_actions.rationale: Reduces the surge of queries that likely caused CPU and connection spikes, mitigating impact while root cause is clarified.

recommended_actions.action: Increase ledger-db connection pool max size (e.g., raise from current setting to 250) and restart order-service to apply.
recommended_actions.rationale: If pool saturation (H3) is the cause, a larger pool will prevent queuing and timeouts.

recommended_actions.action: Collect and enable order-service request rate, CPU, and memory metrics; enable detailed ledger-db connection pool usage metrics.
recommended_actions.rationale: Fills critical data gaps needed to confirm or refute traffic surge vs. pool saturation hypotheses.

recommended_actions.action: Review and, if necessary, revert the autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor change (cfg-2903) after confirming its impact.
recommended_actions.rationale: Although current evidence (no autovacuum warnings) does not strongly support H1, reverting removes a potential contributor.

recommended_actions.action: Implement alerting on ledger-db CPU >80 % and active connections >150 to trigger automated scaling or throttling.
recommended_actions.rationale: Prevents recurrence by providing early warning of resource exhaustion.

recommended_actions.action: Perform capacity planning for ledger-db, including I/O and network latency monitoring, and consider scaling resources.
recommended_actions.rationale: Addresses underlying resource limits that could cause both H2 and H3 scenarios.

data_gaps: Missing order-service resource metrics (CPU %, memory %, request rate) for the incident window.
Missing ledger-db connection pool configuration details (max size, current usage) and per‑connection wait time metrics.
No ledger-db I/O throughput (disk read/write) data to assess possible I/O bottleneck.
No network latency measurements between order-service and ledger-db during the incident.
what_would_change_the_conclusion: A verified spike in order-service request rate coinciding with the latency onset would strongly support hypothesis H2 (traffic‑driven resource exhaustion).
Evidence that the configured connection pool max size is below 180 connections (e.g., config dump) would validate hypothesis H3 (pool saturation).
Logs showing increased autovacuum activity or table bloat metrics would shift confidence toward hypothesis H1.

Shared components used by order-service downstream include ledger-db (Postgres), redis-cache, and kafka, all marked as shared in the dependency graph.
